body:
> Which "developers" do you think are using it?

I think few people use it today, but that's likely because of how hard it is to leverage `opt-dist` outside the Rust CI. I think, in the future, it would be used:

* Directly by anyone who wants to package Rust, needs to bootstrap it themselves, and wants to build an optimized dist with PGO+BOLT. Namely, large distros and companies would benefit from this.
* Indirectly by anyone consuming Rust from the above distributors. Namely, folks using Rust from their package manager, and people using Rust at large companies.
author: lovesegfault

body:
For future reference, my argument boils down to:

**premises**

* the point of the `rustc-dev-src` dist tarball is to allow people to bootstrap Rust
* most people bootstrapping Rust want a production-grade toolchain as a result
* the vanilla bootstrap is not sufficient to bootstrap a production-grade rust-toolchain
* it is undesirable for users to be forced to reinvent the wheel and roll their own complex PGO/BOLT bootstrapping pipeline

**therefore**
* it should be possible to bootstrap a production-grade Rust toolchain from the `rustc-dev-src` tarball using `opt-dist`

body:
Out-of-tree kernel builds with read-only source trees are supported and easy to do, so we should be able to do everything in the `Dockerfile` (i.e. clone + `bindgen` with `--locked`), e.g. the following should work even if you do not have permissions into `$LINUX_FOLDER`:

```sh
make -C $LINUX_FOLDER O=$BUILD_FOLDER LLVM=1 -j$(($(nproc) + 1)) \
    rustavailable \
    defconfig

$LINUX_FOLDER/scripts/kconfig/merge_config.sh -O $BUILD_FOLDER -m $BUILD_FOLDER/.config $SOME_PATH/rfl-for-rust-ci.config

make -C $LINUX_FOLDER O=$BUILD_FOLDER LLVM=1 -j$(($(nproc) + 1)) \
    olddefconfig \
    samples/rust/rust_minimal.o \
    samples/rust/rust_print.o \
    drivers/net/phy/ax88796b_rust.o
```

(Even if that were not the case, wouldn't copying the tree to a writable place be better than re-cloning from network and using `bindgen` without `--locked`? A third alternative could be fixing the version of `bindgen` so that we do not need the clone before it, allowing to move the `bindgen` to the `Dockerfile`).

You could also put the `rfl-for-rust-ci.config` into the `Dockerfile`, I guess, but that means we need to rebuild the image if we just change that bit. By the way, how does the `Dockerfile` get re-built? Is it just if any change happens to the file?

body:
Sadly this is business-as-usual for the pretty printer. It has been broken like this for as long as I remember. The exact behavior is hard to characterize but it's something like: comments and blank lines are anchored to a byte offset in the file. In certain supported positions, the pretty printer will check the current byte offset in the _output_ and flush all comments and blank lines that appeared at any lower byte offset in the _input_ and has not already been printed. This is great if a syntax tree is parsed and immediately printed back out unmodified, because most comments can be preserved accurately in that case. But if we're printing output that is not identical to the input (such as because we performed macro-expansion) then the result is bogus.

It's also why I am using `///` throughout this file instead of `//`. Attributes are anchored correctly to syntax tree nodes as opposed to byte locations.

body:
What if a distro wants to drop Rust lld binaries and rely on system lld?

Then the corresponding `self-contained` directories either won't exist or will be empty.
If we just push the `-B` options without checking then gcc will go through them and then proceed searching and finding lld on the system without errors.

If we report an error here, then such distros will also need to reset self-contained flags in target specs to false, probably through env vars like the current `CFG_USE_SELF_CONTAINED_LINKER`.
This will have a negative effect on portability of options like `-Clink-self-contained=+linker` between distros (if we need such portability).

Not having both can be seen as a mismatch, and that situation would be properly modeled as `-Clink-self-contained=-linker -Clinker-features=+lld`.

Note that, for small N, it's not obvious at all to me that this is necessarily a win.  Zero-initializing a `[ascii::Char; 8]` for example is just a single `0_u64`, and having it be `MaybeUninit` instead comes with the cost of it not getting `noundef` when it's passed around, reducing optimization possibilities for what LLVM can do with it.

For large, especially heap-allocated buffers it can help to avoid initializing them, but making all this code safety-critical (`EscapeIterInner::ascii` now has to be considered for understanding if it's UB, for example) is not at all obvious that it's a good tradeoff.

body:
There's analogue of `DefPathHash` for expansion ids called `ExpnHash`.
It was introduced in https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/pull/87044 and https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/pull/86676 (you may be interested in reading those threads).

This hash is stable in the sense that it is suitable for working with multiple compilations, but it is probably less resistant to small changes in code than `DefPathHash` (https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/pull/86676#issuecomment-877489460).
Although it may be more resistant now than back in 2021 because spans going into the incremental system are item-relative now.

Getting performance improvements from incremental expansion reuse *may* require using some other more change-resistant hashing scheme.
author: petrochenkov

body:
> Although it may be more resistant now than back in 2021 because spans going into the incremental system are item-relative now.

Only starting from HIR, right? Macro expansion is before HIR lowering.

> Getting performance improvements from incremental expansion reuse may require using some other more change-resistant hashing scheme.

An option is a stencil mechanism like in Cranelift. Basically you split both the macro expansion input into a stencil and stencil parameters. Any external reference which doesn't affect macro expansion (like spans assuming no unstable features to introspect spans are used) are stored in the stencil parameters and the stencil refers to them by an index into the stencil parameters. And after macro expansion you combine the expansion result and the stencil parameters again to get a regular `TokenStream`. Only the stencil needs to be hashed. If an external reference changes, the stencil parameters will change too, but the offset into the stencil parameters as stored in the stencil itself remains the same, so the cache will not be invalidated.

https://docs.rs/cranelift-codegen/latest/cranelift_codegen/ir/function/struct.FunctionParameters.html

I think we could add layout-aware scalar-pair constructors (and destructors) that work like <https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/blob/54cdc13542ef548e7d7f71cd48cc9e4f239e0e25/compiler/rustc_codegen_ssa/src/mir/rvalue.rs#L713-L724> if we needed to.

But yeah, no need to do that for now, and the way we do layout optimizations for structs we put bigger, higher-alignment types first anyway, so `(T, bool)` will I think always be in that order anyway right now.

(Or we could add a `repr(linear)` type for `WithOverflow<T>` that these could return, if needed, though that seems like overkill.)

body: Should this be allowed when doing scoped thread spawning? Lazy spawning in a thread pool wouldn't use scoped thread spawning and denying `no_hooks` for scoped thread spawning could potentially allow `!Send` types to depend on thread local storage existing on all threads that can access it. For example if you have a C library which needs to be initialized on every thread, you may be able to pass a token around indicating that it is initialized and install a spawn hook to initialize it on every new thread. Then a `Sync + !Send` token would allow accessing the C api on child threads without having to check for initialization. This example may be a bit contrived though.

The compiler and the used C++ standard library are independent. gcc will usually use libstdc++ of the same version (but isn't required). clang on Linux will usually use *some* libstdc++ version -- in this case the compiler version and libstdc++ version have no relation at all. clang on other platforms like macos will use libc++, in which case the clang version and libc++ version will likely match. > --crate-type=lib, #![crate_type = "lib"] - A Rust library will be produced. This is an ambiguous concept as to what exactly is produced because a library can manifest itself in several forms. body:
It's intentional. You could definitely argue that it is bad, if you want. 

I added the behavior of immediately exiting on the second ctrl-c because I thought it would be the obvious thing to try if the compiler didn't respond to the first. At least the most recent issue https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/issues/125428 indicates this is either not obvious or prevented in some scenarios.

100 ms is a long time for a program, but significantly shorter than even an athlete's reaction time. Unless the OS scheduler truly hates us, the process should exit before the user even has time to realize the process didn't immediately exit and send a second ctrl-c.

body:
cc https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/pull/103413#discussion_r1616312771

"Currently, adding a field of type `PhantomData<T>` indicates that your type *owns* data of type `T` in very rare circumstances" is intentional. Adding `PhantomData<T>` to your type only impacts whether your type 'owns' `T` in rare circumstances: if your type already has another field which requires drop:

```rust
struct DoesNotOwnT<T> {
   field: *const T,
   phantom_data: PhantomData<T>,
}
```

```rust
struct DoesOwnT<T> {
   field: *const T,
   other_field: String,
   phantom_data: PhantomData<T>,
}
```

We need the `private_candidate` field to communicate an actually found candidate out to the `pick` method. While we could just eagerly return the `PrivateMatch` error, that would mean we'd miss out on suggesting traits that could be imported to get access to another method of the same name.

Of course we could just eagerly report (not return) an error from method selection and return that no methods were found, which will subsequently return an error containing the list of traits that should be imported. But then method selection is reporting errors, which is also not be desirable (and probably wrong in various cases where we'll return a better error later).

body:
Clippy only ever calls `eq_assoc_type_binding` for parenthesized generic args (`Trait(Ty0, Ty1, ...) -> RetTy`) whose lowered form is guaranteed to contain a single associated type binding, namely for the associated type `Output`).

I'm not saying that those unwraps are great, they certainly aren't. However, this change is entirely semantics-preserving as `TypeBinding::ty` on master panics if the assoc item constraint isn't an assoc ty equality constraint. I've made method `ty` non-panicking / return an `Option` instead, hence the need to unwrap here.

body:
> Doesn't this require an additional dependency to be installed?

As the patch stands today, it requires libzstd.so to be available at runtime if libzstd was available at build time. It doesn't actually require libzstd to be available at build time (because it uses ON instead of FORCE_ON).

There's a matrix of possible outcomes here.

|| ON | FORCE_ON|
|-|-----|-------------|
| No LLVM_USE_STATIC_ZSTD | Not required at build time, required at runtime if present at build time, silently disabled if not present at build time | Required at build time and runtime|
| LLVM_USE_STATIC_ZSTD | Not required at build time or runtime, silently disabled if not present at build time | Required at  build time, not at runtime|

Where we're currently in the top left cell.

body:
Ok, so to do a final `try` build and perf run, we'd also need to install the dependencies on the dist builder, [here](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/blob/master/src/ci/docker/host-x86_64/dist-x86_64-linux/Dockerfile).

---

Overall I'm not fond of the current behavior of implicitly enabling the feature if the dependency is present on the system. It's not clear this will happen nor is it documented; no tests would fail if there's a regression/mistake/evolution on the builders, etc.

Ideally, we'd at least:
- have opt-ins in the config and bootstrap, which would fail when activated but the dependency isn't found.
- document these
- extend our testing infra to have `//@needs-compression-$format` directives, so we can correctly test all the supported cases we expect
- and finally we'd enable the opt-ins on our test/dist builders

That being said, we don't *have* to do all this in this PR if you don't have time to do it. It's not a tiny amount of work.

I don't know how others feel about this, but it seems fine to land this PR's strategy if it's clearly documented in the PR title and body, in bootstrap, and where the dependencies are installed, and we can take it the rest of the way.

The lint implementation looks fine. But I'm surprised by the following.
- This lint is `allow` by default.
- It's only enabled for miri.
- But miri doesn't use `group_imports = "StdExternalCrate"`.
- So the places where a `self::` prefix is added don't cause any `use` reorderings.

I.e. as used, it requires `self::` prefixes but does not group `use` declarations more accurately, which doesn't seem like an improvement. It would make more sense if the lint was enabled for parts of the code that use `group_imports = "StdExternalCrate"`.

body:
> I think we need to look at the obligation to re-derive the `FulfillmentErrorCode` -- perhaps look at how the FulfillmentErrorCode is created in the first place in the old solver?

I'm not sure if that is easily possible with the old solver. As far as I understand these `FulfillmentErrorCode` are produced somewhat ad hoc in the code here that does the actual solving: 

https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/blob/f2e1a3a80ae54734e1a3d306f31c2caebb05de9b/compiler/rustc_trait_selection/src/traits/fulfill.rs#L745-L750

At this point we know the following things about the passed obligation:

* If it changes it does contain a unimplemented trait requirement somewhere in the stack as `#[do_not_recommend]` an only applied to trait impls (That's asserted at other places).
* I think we can only ever end up with changing anything here for `FulfillmentErrorCode::Project` or `FulfillmentErrorCode::Project`. In both cases it will change it to the a trait requirement not implemented obligation due to where `do_not_recommend` can be placed. 

Maybe it's a good idea to just explicitly check the `FulfillmentErrorCode` before if its `FulfillmentErrorCode::Select(Unimplementd)` or `FulfillmentErrorCode::Project` so that it always matches that assumptions? 


> For the record, I haven't looked deep enough to see if this is possible to turn into a weird diagnostic (or an ICE), so you may need to do a bit of research yourself.

At least all of the compiler test suite (via `./x.py test`) runs fine with this change. That said I will try to produce a few edge cases with the `#[do_not_recommend]` attribute added and add them as well to the tests.

body:
Problem: this logic is wrong for the multi-output case (for the final `remove_file` that is asserted to be successful, not the highlighted one here). When you request multiple output artifacts via `--emit=asm,obj`, rustc has to produce at least two separate output artifact files. This mandates that the different kinds of output artifacts cannot be in the same file, and so they are actually named `{output_file}.s` and `{output_file}.o` respectively. But in the one-output-kind case, rustc can omit the extension and use the output filename via `-o` as provided. I missed this during the review of the original port, sorry!

This is why you observe

> As demonstrated, not commenting out the last case results in `the file in path ""/checkout/obj/build/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/test/run-make/reset-codegen-1/reset-codegen-1/rmake_out/multi-output"" could not be removed.: Os { code: 2, kind: NotFound, message: "No such file or directory" }`

Yeah, the reason for using drop bombs was two-fold:

1. `#[must_use]` was not sufficient to guarantee that constructed command wrappers are *eventually* actually executed.
2. `#[must_use]` was noisy on intermediate builder methods (especially if a builder method wants to be conditionally called).
author: jieyouxu

body:
I feel like this is different from "normal" code:

- I would not `#[deny(unused_must_use)]` for normal code (e.g. rustc), because there are often cases where it is noisy and it's better checked at CI to avoid blocking local dev.
- But for these rmake.rs tests, they are often short, and not using `#[must_use]` values are almost always bugs and are esepecially bad if that allows the test to silently pass. That is, imo, if the test author *really* wants to not use a `#[must_use]` value, they should probably `let _ = must_use()` or something better.

I'm not opposed to making this respect `deny-warnings = false` in `config.toml`, but if I'm running tests locally I personally *want* them to fail fast due to `-Dunused_must_use` instead of waiting for PR CI.

body:
Yes: the answer is that this `#[track_caller]` is actually load-bearing for the panic message's line number:

Test rmake.rs:

```
use run_make_support::bare_rustdoc;

fn main() {
    bare_rustdoc();
}
```

produces

```
thread 'main' panicked at src/tools/run-make-support/src/drop_bomb/mod.rs:43:13:
command constructed but not executed at line 4: `/home/gh-jieyouxu/rust/build/aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu/stage1/bin/rustdoc`
note: run with `RUST_BACKTRACE=1` environment variable to display a backtrace
```

without the `#[track_caller]` on the `bare_rustdoc` (and transitively `Rustdoc::bare`), the line number is for rustdoc.rs inside the support library

```
thread 'main' panicked at src/tools/run-make-support/src/drop_bomb/mod.rs:43:13:
command constructed but not executed at line 10: `/home/gh-jieyouxu/rust/build/aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu/stage1/bin/rustdoc`
note: run with `RUST_BACKTRACE=1` environment variable to display a backtrace
```

I could/should adjust the panic info on the drop bomb to contain and thus report the complete `std::panic::Location` instead of just the line number.
author: jieyouxu

body:
In addition, I think it is worth also clarifying that for `r: &mut T`, `from_ref(r)` is equivalent to `from_ref(r as &T)` which is *not* guaranteed to be equivalent to `r as *const` and is *not*  necessarily safer than `r as const T`, in particular if the resulting pointer will ever be cast to a `*mut _` pointer. Maybe there is similar nuance for `r: Deref<T>`.

However, https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/type-coercions.html#coercion-types does seem to say that when `r: &mut T`, `r as *const T` is equivalent to `(r as &T) as *const T` since there is no coercion rule for `&mut T to *const T`. So first we should decide whether we can really make the potentially-backward-incompatible change to add a `&mut T` to `*const T` coercion rule, because if we decide we can't, then this new wording isn't necessary.
author: briansmith

body:
>  for `r: &mut T`, `r as *const T` is equivalent to `(r as &T) as *const T` since there is no coercion rule for `&mut T to *const T`. 

Actually, `r as *const T` could also be `(r as *mut T) as *const T`, so I guess some clarification is needed.
author: briansmith

body:
I don't think this is the right place to discuss the semantics of coercions. They behave the same everywhere, surely we don't want to explain them in each function that takes a reference. (e.g. `slice.as_ptr()` has exactly the same questions).

I also don't see why this PR should be blocked on https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/issues/56604. That issue is long-standing so I don't expect it to be resolved soon, this clarification however is necessary short-term according to yourself as you said it is ambiguous.

>  then this new wording isn't necessary.

IMO the new wording is not *necessary* under any ruleset, since `r` is declared `&T` and so that's the only case the docs care about. As I already pointed out, for `r` of arbitrary type there are counterexamples to the equivalence. So the alternative interpretation would be something like "for all `r` where both expressions type-check, `from_ref(r)` is equivalent to `r as *const T`", which is quite far from what the text says and it needs to conjure a fresh `T` out of nothing -- IMO clear enough signals that this is *not* the intended interpretation.
author: RalfJung

body:
It's analogous to the situation for `addr_of!`, which has a similar caveat:
> Note that Deref/Index coercions (and their mutable counterparts) are applied inside `addr_of_mut!` like everywhere else, in which case a reference is created to call `Deref::deref` or `Index::index`, respectively. The statements above only apply when no such coercions are applied.

In both cases, the construct is designed to make things safer, but not understanding the interaction with coercions is especially dangerous.

body:
I am very confused by `expr_into_dest`.

Ignoring that opaque types require drop even if their hidden type don't means that the destination of stuff like `ExprKind::Borrow` would now add a drop, and more importantly, tries to remove a drop in `unschedule_drop`, `expr_into_dest` **has to** schedule the drop for `dest` to be the last drop in the given scope. If it does not, we just ICE when trying to unschedule the drop for the destination in matches/if else.

I've added an assert that stuff could get unscheduled and it always passes, see https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/commit/a57f57bf00af66f89c5ecf66d8dec9874cb18301

While this PR should probably go through as-is to get the fix in as soon as possible, I feel like this system is somewhat brittle, relying on specifically the symbol `rustc_deprecated_safe_2024` and the edition being hard coded to check at least `2024`.  I wonder if it would be a good idea for a follow up PR to somehow make this general in that the attribute could specify an edition in which a function starts becoming unsafe, and check that edition?

However, such a followup assumes that we will make more functions `unsafe` in  the future due to oversight.  Ideally we don't have to do that, and I think that the current state of things is such that just about everything has been audited?  So perhaps it's not worth such a generalization, since it ideally doesn't happen again.

body:
Just my 2 cents: I prefer the style where you just use `pub` in the internal modules, and then limit visibility in the parent (for multiple reasons, one of them being that `pub(crate)` is IMO too verbose). It seems to be more uniform to me, in the sense that you export things from the module, and then decide in the parent what to export further and what not to export, rather than hard-coding the visibility to the whole crate in nested modules.

For example, in `rustc_ast_lowering/src/lib.rs`, all modules are actually private, and the crate selectively exports (or declares as `pub` in the root library module) just a few selected items. It doesn't seem to me that adding `pub(crate)` to many items in the nested modules (which are not reexported from the crate anyway) adds a lot of value.

Incidentally, I was able to track down why these tests require stage 2 in ui-fulldeps.

It's because #110478 made “stage 1” tests in ui-fulldeps actually use the *stage 0* compiler, so the test tries to use an in-tree compiler (via API) with a bootstrap sysroot, and predictably fails.

I have an idea of how to solve this (pass along two sysroots and let fulldeps tests select the correct one), but I haven't decided whether it's worth the extra complexity.

body:
Cool, thanks for this!

I don't know how much back-and-forth you want to do on this PR, vs iterative improvements on our CI scripts and documentations, and fuchsia's "build from rust CI" setup, but apart from the comments I left here, and what you've added in https://github.com/rust-lang/rustc-dev-guide/pull/1989, here's a list I remember having issues with:

As non-fuchsia engineers, we'll unfortunately need some hand-holding with the build system. We don't know what we can do with `fx`, if we're to use it or not, how common cargo use-cases translate, etc. Nor do we know the actual fuchsia components to build, or how to discover them, when an issue appears in one of them. Some description about all this would be nice. Otherwise, we're kind of randomly mixing paths and names found in some "build.gn" files, fx expectedly not finding the component, but also not saying which components Levenshtein-match what was requested. 

The first thing you **need** to do when debugging an issue in the builder is to remove `--quiet` from https://fuchsia.googlesource.com/fuchsia/+/refs/heads/releases/canary/scripts/rust/build_fuchsia_from_rust_ci.sh#118. It's understandable that we don't want to show huge logs for CI (though maybe it's not that costly I don't know, and am not on t-infra), but it would be helpful for people debugging issues to have _some_ output locally. What could work is that only our CI workflows add the `--quiet`, so that local use-cases with `src/ci/docker/run.sh x86_64-gnu-integration` would not themselves hide fuchsia's logs.

(Actually, maybe the first thing is to setup one's local rustc checkout to even run the CI docker scripts in general, where IIUC the most common initial hurdle is that some submodules need to be initialized and checked out. CI does this automatically but it's usually not the case for developers).

I also needed a way to change rustc's arguments when building a crate -- otherwise I had to introduce an error in fuchsia code, to extract the command-line used and change it, and stop using the build system afterwards. I don't know if it's possible to with `fx` (e.g. if I can use `RUSTFLAGS`, or if there is some equivalent to the `cargo check + cargo rustc` combination to only override a leaf crate's arguments. I expect this to be very common in practice, and any way to make this easy will be helpful. Maybe some documentation on how to do this today would also be enough, for example.

This is more a QOL thing, but I noticed a few things being built which were surprising, but surely useful for you. In any case, maybe it'd make builds slightly faster to not have: 
- 3 targets (x64, fuchsia, wasm, -- w/ fuchsia being the default for the build when maybe the most useful one locally is the host target, so that artifacts can be used from outside the docker container),
- or the cranelift backend being built (I'm almost positive I saw some cg_clif build logs even though only cg_llvm seems to be setup),
- and checking which stage is built and used. Here I expect also some of suboptimal bootstrap + tools stage versioning mismatch to come into play. To overapproximate the situation, and I don't know that it really applies I'd need to check, here's an example: if you build "stage 2 rustdoc", it will build the stage 2 compiler + std, but actually link with stage 1. Fuchsia is using clippy, and maybe it works similarly. If that's the case, then avoiding building an unused stage 2 would be nice. Though avoiding the need to build clippy in the first place could also be good for people working on the compiler I guess, e.g. if locally we could choose to use an fx equivalent of cargo check instead of fx clippy.

I though putting `DUMMY_SP` as the primary span would be an un-allowed case (resulting in an ICE) but apparently it's only the case when putting dummy spans for suggestions.

Currently putting a dummy span forces our default error emitter to attach the diagnostic to the crate outermost file, which implies having `ERROR` annotations (unsure of their usefulness here).

<details>

```diff
{
    "$message_type": "diagnostic",
    "children": [
        {
            "children": [
            ],
            "code": null,
            "level": "note",
            "message": "config `windows` is only supposed to be controlled by `--target`",
            "rendered": null,
            "spans": [
            ]
        },
        {
            "children": [
            ],
            "code": null,
            "level": "note",
            "message": "see <https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/issues/xxxxx> for more information",
            "rendered": null,
            "spans": [
            ]
        },
        {
            "children": [
            ],
            "code": null,
            "level": "note",
            "message": "`#[deny(unexpected_builtin_cfgs)]` on by default",
            "rendered": null,
            "spans": [
            ]
        }
    ],
    "code": {
        "code": "unexpected_builtin_cfgs",
        "explanation": null
    },
    "level": "error",
    "message": "unexpected `--cfg windows` flag",
    "rendered": "error: unexpected `--cfg windows` flag\n   |\n   = note: config `windows` is only supposed to be controlled by `--target`\n   = note: see <https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/issues/xxxxx> for more information\n   = note: `#[deny(unexpected_builtin_cfgs)]` on by default\n\n",
    "spans": [
+        {
+            "byte_end": 0,
+            "byte_start": 0,
+            "column_end": 1,
+            "column_start": 1,
+            "expansion": null,
+            "file_name": "[..]/rust/tests/ui/cfg/disallowed-cli-cfgs.rs",
+            "is_primary": true,
+            "label": null,
+            "line_end": 1,
+            "line_start": 1,
+            "suggested_replacement": null,
+            "suggestion_applicability": null,
+            "text": [
+            ]
+        }
    ]
}
```

</details>

Conceptually idk if it makes sense to have the diag attached to the crate since at the  point we lint the crate doesn't even exist yet. I also find it slightly better to not use a dummy span in diag since as can be seen here it result in some unexpected behaviours, which is probably fine when it's a mistake or when something went wrong but doesn't seem clean here IMO.

Another thing, it's currently not handled by the `annotate_snippet` emitter, which currently completely ignores any diag if the primary is a dummy span, cf. https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/blob/d371d17496f2ce3a56da76aa083f4ef157572c20/compiler/rustc_errors/src/annotate_snippet_emitter_writer.rs#L139-L142

body:
> I don't have big-endian hardware to verify this, so I could only validate this in Miri. However, AFAIK the intent is that the two ways of representing the result are equal-up-to-transmute, and it is clearly the case that `0b1101001010u16` transmutes to `[0b11, 0b01001010]`.

afaik the intent is actually to match what llvm does when bitcasting from e.g. `<10 x i1>` to `i10`.

you can likely use llvm const propagation to test how llvm behaves by compiling for some big-endian target and comparing the optimized llvm-ir to just returning a constant. alternatively, setting up a chroot with a different arch using debootstrap and qemu-user isn't that hard on linux, though llvm's backends may have bugs around weird vector lengths.
author: programmerjake

body:
Looking at [codegen for this intrinsic](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/blob/a9702a66684f0e1f412d92a83761be2e461b69fb/compiler/rustc_codegen_llvm/src/intrinsic.rs#L1379-L1390), I am a bit confused: for an input vector of length 10, it seems to expect an `i10` return type -- but that's impossible (and contradicts the docs), the return type is `i16`. So I don't understand how [this case](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/blob/a9702a66684f0e1f412d92a83761be2e461b69fb/compiler/rustc_codegen_llvm/src/intrinsic.rs#L1423-L1426) can ever be hit for larger-than-8 non-power-of-2 vectors.

However, for arrays things seem quite clear -- we first zero-extend to `expected_bytes * 8`, which in this case is i16 and will result in 0b0000001101001010, and then that gets transmuted to `[u8; 2]` (via alloca, store, load) which will result in `[0b00000011, 0b01001010]`.
author: RalfJung

body: Something else is also odd about the implementation -- it goes through some lengths to specifically return the most significant bit (MSB) of each lane, but the docs for the intrinsic say that the input vector must contain only `0` and `!0` so we could just return any bit -- the lshr that the intrinsic generates seems entirely unnecessary.
author: RalfJung

body:
> So I don't understand how [this case](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/blob/a9702a66684f0e1f412d92a83761be2e461b69fb/compiler/rustc_codegen_llvm/src/intrinsic.rs#L1423-L1426) can ever be hit for larger-than-8 non-power-of-2 vectors.

Lol, turns out it indeed cannot be hit. Miri implements the docs as written but codegen is buggy -- see [this test](https://play.rust-lang.org/?version=nightly&mode=debug&edition=2021&gist=af9900c577ccb5ccae6b5aef2841c6a5).

If this becomes a helper, then `cc` should receive a rework. I can't really name this `object_file_name` or such, because it provides no extension for the MSVC platform and `.o` for others. The reason for this isn't that MSVC object files have no extension - it's that `cc` automatically appends `.obj` to output filenames. Once `cc` is done, then I need to manually add `.obj` to the filename, or else `llvm_ar` will complain, as that one *doesn't* automatically append extensions.

There is some inconsistency like this around the run_make_support library. For example, `rustc` will not auto-append `.rs` to input files, but `run` will auto-append `.exe` to input files if on Windows.

I feel like doing this rework (which would change a lot of test files too) would be better suited to a different PR.

I'm not quite sure what you mean. My comment has nothing to do with somehow supporting tests that use both `#![no_std]` and `test_harness`. I'm just suggesting a way we can merge more doctests than the current implementation does.

The current implementation in this PR looks at each test together with the args passed to rustdoc and decides which tests are mergeable and which must be compiled and run on their own. Then it merges all mergeable tests into one file for each edition, since obviously doctests of different editions can't be in the same rustc invocation. It considers tests that use the langstring `test_harness` (which allows using `#[test]` in a doctest) or the attribute `#![no_std]` to be unmergeable (standalone). I'm suggesting that we instead allow merging these tests, but only with other tests that match their combination of relevant attributes (edition, `no_std`, `test_harness`, etc.) and are thus compatible.

Please let me know if I misunderstood your comment.

body:
This still-pretty-noisy signature cannot reuse `ChangeOutputType` without falling afoul of either the `type_alias_bounds` lint or having an _even more grody_ `<<T as Try>::Residual as Residual<blahblahblah>>::TryType`.

One option that we do have that requires slightly more implementation work (changing the internals of the ones that use NeverShortCircuit, mostly) is this:
```rust
    #[unstable(feature = "array_try_map", issue = "79711")]
    pub fn try_map<R>(
        self,
        f: impl FnMut(T) -> R,
    ) -> impl Try<Output = [R::Output; N], Residual = R::Residual>
    where
        R: Try<Residual: Residual<[R::Output; N]>>,
```

Even further alternates might exist, but I think most of them involve sitting down for a good while and thinking very hard about how the traits relate to each other.

author: tbu-

body:
> I agree that suggesting `let _ = ...` is a bit silly when the `drop` argument has an explicit `&`. It's more reasonable for something like `drop(ref);`.

`let _ = …` makes sense as a replacement when it actually drops something, e.g. for `let _ = func_call()`. `let _ = variable_containing_mut_ref;` is not useful as a replacement because it does exactly nothing, it simply matches the always matching pattern against the variable. The variable is not made inaccessible.
author: tbu-

body:
> The variable is not made inaccessible.

That was never the point. The point of the lint is to signal users that the `drop` call does not drop the underline value.

Whenever or not the variable after the suggestion is made inaccessible is IMO completely irrelevant to the issue that the lint is trying to point at.

> `let _ = …` makes sense as a replacement when it actually drops something

Or as a way to suppress to the "unused variable" lint, as was called out by T-lang in https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/pull/109732#issuecomment-1496414416.
author: Urgau

body:
> > So it's the "does nothing" part that is the problem here? I.e. it's not true for mutable references?
> 
> Yes.

IMO, this isn't true, the call to `std::mem::drop` with a reference (mutable or not) does nothing *to the reference or the underline value*. The fact that is does something to the binding/variable it-self is unfortunate but IMO irrelevant here.

------

> How about just changing the message to this: "a call to `std::mem::drop` that is passed a reference drops the reference, not the underlying value".

I would personally prefer: "calls to `std::mem::drop` with a reference does not drop the underline value"
author: Urgau

body:
> > `let _ = …` makes sense as a replacement when it actually drops something
> 
> Or as a way to suppress to the "unused variable" lint, as was called out by T-lang in [#109732 (comment)](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/pull/109732#issuecomment-1496414416).

Yes. I think this should be a conscious decision though. `let _ = variable;` signals to the reader that the programmer wanted to explicitly silence the unused variable lint. Perhaps we could mention that in the replacement hint? "If you just want to mark the variable as used, use `let _ = variable`?

body:
Discussion: these APIs looks a bit weird to me for a couple of reasons:

- It's based on globbing which can be surprising if you don't document the edge cases, and even then it's not immediately obvious how the implementation behaves.
- It uses `dynamic_lib_name` et al. on constructed glob patterns, which seems a bit weird to me, I think it's cleaner if we extract out `dynamic_lib_extension` that's used by both `dynamic_lib_name` and the fs walker to determine what files to remove.
- The count APIs are *especially* weird because I think it's almost an anti-pattern, for vast majority of tests I would expected that we control and know *exactly* which output artifacts we generate. Not checking for those (e.g. by removing the expected output artifacts) almost smell like bugs.

Maybe take a look at how tidy does filewalking (e.g. <https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/blob/master/src/tools/tidy/src/walk.rs>) for inspiration, but we definitely don't want to directly mimic tidy's interfaces. 

I think it's easier to understand if we implement it in terms of `walkdir` or some other variant of explicit filesystem walk, and document if it is recursive or not.

What do you think?

body:
I've reproduced the pre-existing logic precisely and it tracks the old span.
It's pretty counter intuitive, but it may indeed be correct? We are effectively taking the old span's absolute position (which needs tracking) and produce a new span with a new parent out of it.
Similarly to https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/pull/126544/files#r1641782800 I'm also not sure.
author: petrochenkov

body:
Yes, we should track the old span. When the old span has a parent, it encodes the absolute lo/hi byte positions, but incr. comp. is convinced it only encodes positions relative to the parent. If we output a span with no parent, incr. comp. will see those absolute positions appear out of thin air.
So we need to tell incr. comp. that we are accessing the absolute positions with `SPAN_TRACK`. The only case when it's not required is when `parent == old_parent`.

I think the problem might be that we introduce the checks multiple times:
`from_size_align` calls `is_size_align_valid` and then calls `from_size_align_unchecked`, which calls `is_size_align_valid` itself. And `is_size_align_valid` calls `is_power_of_two` and then `Alignment::new_unchecked` which calls `is_power_of_two` again. And `Alignment::new_unchecked` is also called in `Layout::from_size_align_unchecked` so `is_power_of_two` is called 5 times in total! Obviously the optimizer will figure this out, but still, we shouldn't even generate that MIR. Could you try using `transmute`s here to create the `Alignment` once the checks have completed and maybe also in `Alignment::new`?

> the check you want is "does this have unevaluated const arg of DefKind::AnonConst"

So basically visiting the `Ty` and check if it has any `UnevaluatedConst`s where `tcx.def_kind($.def.0) == DefKind::AnonConst`? Sure I can do that.

Yeah, I figured that the way (M)GCEs are resolved and dealt with will likely change significantly. Hence the `FIXME(generic_const_exprs): Revisit this before stabilization`. I just really wanted to add a test for this relatively surprising behavior just so ppl working on (M)GCE have something tangible to work with. I don't particularly care right now how the final behavior will look like as long as various edge cases are considered :^)

body:
Latest push uses `pthread_self` and `Mutex<Option<pthread_t>>` instead of `libc::gettid` and `AtomicI32` for maximum portability[^1]. This also removes the code duplication since there is no "fallback" implementation. Given that this code should not be hot, I think it should be fine to not use atomics here.

One possible issue is that *formally*, comparing `pthread_t`s is supposed to use [`pthread_equal`](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man3/pthread_equal.3.html), not `==` comparison, but the `libc` crate currently does not expose `pthread_equal`. I don't know if any supported libcs *actually* make `pthread_equal` do anything  other than `==`, though, so it might just be fine (glibc and musl both appear to implement `pthread_equal` as `==` (glibc) ([musl](https://github.com/bminor/musl/blob/ab31e9d6a0fa7c5c408856c89df2dfb12c344039/include/pthread.h#L92))). Alternately, we could just have a one-off `extern "C" { fn pthread_equal(...) -> ...; }` above the call, at least until/unless `libc` exposes `pthread_equal`.

[^1]:  since `pthread_t` is different on different Linux platforms: `*-unknown-linux-gnu` appears to have it as `c_ulong` (which is `u64` on 64-bit and `u32` on 32-bit), `*-unknown-linux-musl` appears to have it as `*mut c_void`, and `*-linux-android` appears to have it as `c_long`

body:
> There's also `libc::pause` which is basically what we need here. It sleeps forever.

I am not sure it does.

From `pause(2)`[^2]:
 
> `pause()` causes  the calling process (or thread) to sleep until a signal is delivered that either terminates the process or causes the invocation of a signal-catching function.
> `pause()` returns only when a signal was caught and the signal-catching function returned.  In this case, `pause()` returns -1, `errno` is set to `EINTR`.

From `pause(3p)`[^3p]:

> The `pause()` function shall suspend the calling thread until delivery of a signal whose action is either to execute a signal-catching function or to terminate the process.
> If the action is to terminate the process, `pause()` shall not return.
> If the action is to execute a signal-catching function, `pause()` shall return after the signal-catching function returns.


[^2]: https://www.man7.org/linux/man-pages/man2/pause.2.html
[^3p]: https://www.man7.org/linux/man-pages/man3/pause.3p.html

body:
> I don’t see any reason to commit to that at this time.

After playing around with this more, I agree. I realized that there are already trait-changing casts which are NOPs at runtime, namely when the supertrait vtable is a prefix of the subtrait vtable. We compile these casts to a NOP but we don't want to allow people to do this as a transmute; the fact that this is a NOP is an implementation detail. The same applies to this case: semantically, `Debug + Send` to `Send` is still a meaningful cast, even if we compile it to a NOP.

We do currently make `Debug + Send` to `Debug` a non-meaningful cast; vtables in Miri only keep track of the principal trait. Maybe that is something we should reconsider, to be fully consistent.

Assuming this comment is about this code: (The PR has changed some since this comment was posted and I'm not sure how good GitHub is at tracking comments across revisions)

        // Please note the order of the check here, the edition is not check on every

> rustmft would only regroup within a contiguous sequence of use statements

Depends what you mean by "contiguous sequence". Blank lines and comments don't act as separators between use statements. Other items (e.g. `mod`, type declarations) do.

And "for the validation errors" seems like a low-value comment to me.
author: nnethercote

body:
> Blank lines and comments don't act as separators between use statements.

For blank lines that makes sense since the entire point is for rustfmt to do the grouping. But for comments I find this highly disruptive.

> And "for the validation errors" seems like a low-value comment to me.

As a maintainer and one of the main authors of this file, I disagree. The imports that carry this comment are unusual, usually we'd not have `*` imports of an enum at a global level, nor `as` aliases. So it's worth explaining why we do something strange like that.

body: I find it rather concerning that we should entirely lose the ability to add a comment to a group of `use` statements. The standard library also has several of these cases show up in this PR, where comments that are helpful to structure the file are now being erased because we have a tool that can't deal with them. That's a bad reason to remove comments from code.

author: cuviper

body:
I think having a group of code with empty lines before and after it, and a comment at the top of it, makes it fairly clear to a human reader that the comment applies to the entire group. But rustfmt is frequently bad at dealing with comments and likes to move them around in ways that change their meaning (https://github.com/rust-lang/rustfmt/issues/3255, https://github.com/rust-lang/rustfmt/issues/3994, https://github.com/rust-lang/rustfmt/issues/5485), so it is no surprise that this happens here, too.  It is a constant frustration of mine that issues like that are ignored in the name of the Grand Goal Of Consistency. For basic rustfmt formatting the advantages it provides are so big that the overall tradeoff still comes out in favor of rustfmt (though it is unfortunate that fixing these rustfmt issues is nobody's priority), but for `use` statements I am not convinced that there's a significant enough problem here worth solving.

> In summary, rustfmt does just fine with like 99.99% of cases and for 0.01% of cases we have a slightly suboptimal experience

That "one in 10000" number is complete guesswork on your end. A couple dozen cases in around 3k source files also shows that you are off by around 2 orders of magnitude.
author: RalfJung

body: There are something like 18,000 use items in `compiler/` and `library/` alone. Maybe the correct number is 99.9% or 99.5%.  No matter what the exact number is, we're having an argument about suboptimal handling of one or two actual comments in the entire codebase. Is that worth blocking this entire change from happening? In my opinion, no.

body: @petrochenkov the primary span label retains that context of the message. I feel like it is bad practice in general to have redundant information in the different parts of the error, and we already get too many complains about "too much text in the errors". This was an attempt to walk that line. In the particular case of "in this scope" you and I know what why that is meaningful, but in practice that wording ends up being more text to say something that is generally implied: if it's not on a specific other scope, it's always "this scope". Whenever we *do* have additional context from "this scope", then it does make sense to mention it ("in trait `Trait`"). If we were to actually *mention* the scope ("cannot find macro `foo` from method `bar`"), that would change my opinion on the use of this (because then the message can be read in isolation without having to read the code to understand the context).

body:
Right, so this is a bit tricky. In general, many of the profilers require some custom configuration of the system, and also some postprocessing. This is documented in [rustc-perf](https://github.com/rust-lang/rustc-perf/tree/master/collector#profiling), and I'm not sure if it is a good idea to duplicate the documentation here.

The tool should let you know exactly what you should do w.r.t. `perf_event_paranoid`, so it is self-documenting in this sense, but if you prefer, we could add a mention of `perf_event_paranoid` (probably to `rustc-perf`?).

Furthermore, even if you run the profiler, it just generates a file on disk and unless you know what to do, it won't be very useful to you. So maybe we could create specific postprocessing steps in bootstrap, for example to open a web browser with the gathered profile after running samply. But even that is not that easy, because what if you run more than one benchmark? :)

Doing profiling and benchmarking does require some specific knowledge at the moment. We could make it easier for the user, but I'm not sure if that code belongs here or into rustc-perf, and how far should we go in this.

body:
This line contains the only observable behavior change in this PR.

https://github.com/rust-lang/rust-clippy/issues/12990 has a writeup of what this code is doing. It is using precedence of the parent expression of an expression `x` to decide whether it's possible to suggest replacing `x` by `&x`, or by `(&x)`.

Precedence of the parent expression is the wrong thing for Clippy to be looking at in this code, and causes the false negatives reported in the link. This PR increases the number of cases which encounter that false negative in the short term, such as `[x; 2]`, but does not make the issue harder to fix in Clippy.

My guess is that at the time the change was made, there were fewer “early” syntactic checks for `let` expressions in bad places, so it was possible for one to (illegally) exist inside certain const contexts that would survive to this point and cause an unwrap panic.

The change from unwrap to if-let was requested by https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/pull/94849#discussion_r833967008, but it doesn't give context for why. I suspect that it would have been preferable to make the None case do a `span_delayed_bug` instead of silently doing nothing.

The comment, code, and `*`/`**`/`~~` changes look correct, but `_`/`__` and `<...>` anchors need the preceding whitespace so snake case doesn't turn into italics (gh agrees with commonmark here):

- `foo*bar*`  foo*bar*
- `foo**bar**`  foo**bar**
- `foo_bar_`  foo_bar_
- `foo__bar__` foo__bar__
- `foo~~bar~`  foo~~bar~~

- `foo<www.docs.rs>` foo<www.docs.rs>

body:
> This seems to assume that the difference between addresses of the two stack variables will never be larger than 3. 

Not really. It assumes that the difference is precisely 0 and non-0 at the same time. The test in question should ALWAYS panic in one place or another (even without the `assert_ne!(i, 0)`). But it doesn't, because some parts gets optimized as if `i` is 0, while others are optimized as if it is not.

What I'm trying to say is that the length choice is arbitrary and that the test will fail no matter the value of `i` (be it 0, or 1, or 3, or 16, or whatever) as long as compiler does not make contradictory assumptions during optimization.

It might actually even break if compiler still makes contradictory assumptions, but optimizes things differently.

The point of the test is to capture the *current* buggy behavior and demonstrate that it can lead to unsoundness in safe code.

@tgross35 
There are a few things needed to create a final target executable with RTEMS. 
One needs the kernel libraries and some linker scripts which can be found via pkg-config files.
The second thing is that one C-file needs to be compiled (with the cross-compiler) which reserves the OS memory depending on a configuration via macro defines.

In order to separate the OS specific parts from the Rust user applications I created a `rtems-sys` crate which figures these things out and forwards it to the crate with the rust application via the "cargo:" commands.

Now, there are different versions of RTEMS where nothing technical would change for the Rust side, except for the linker name, i.e. `arm-rtems7-gcc` instead of `arm-rtems6-gcc`. So, if I set the `linker` variable in the spec to `None` how can I set it to the correct value when compiling the user application? The `rtems-sys` build script has all the information and uses it to pass the needed linker flags to the user application. I just haven't figured out how to also pass the correct linker name.

That was just what came to my mind when writing this at midnight. The warning and note could definitely be better, for example now I'm thinking of this:
```
warning: passing a pointer to asm! block with `nomem` option
 --> $PATH:$LINE
  |
  | core::arch::asm!("mov {p}, {p}", p = in(reg) p, options(nomem, nostack, preserves_flags));
  |                                  ^
  = note: `nomem` must be only used when no memory read or write happens inside the asm! block.
  = note: This is not limited to global variables, it also includes passed pointers.
  = note: If this is intentional, consider casting the pointer to an integer.
  = note: If not, change the `nomem` attribute to `readonly`
```
Warning is concise and note explains in more detail what is going on and how to fix the issue. Of course, depending on the pointer mutability and asm options, they will be a bit different.
author: Soveu

body:
I think this is probably underexplained and should be omitted:
```
  = note: If this is intentional, consider casting the pointer to an integer.
```

Assembly is `unsafe` and we should be careful to eschew recommendations that aren't clearly applicable, because people will blindly take recommendations without thinking hard (no matter how much we would like to believe otherwise).

Further, people who work with assembly often have the interesting belief that pointers and integers are the same thing, so I can imagine someone misunderstanding this and the next line as somehow equivalent:
```
  = note: If this is intentional, consider casting the pointer to an integer.
  = note: If not, change the `nomem` attribute to `readonly`
```

So I think the suggestions should be more conservative, only including:
- remove nomem (as this is safest)
- replace nomem with readonly (less safe, but may be sound)
- allow this lint (would require moving this into the linting framework, but clearly has no soundness impacts)
author: workingjubilee

body: It is probably fine if there's a good way to explain _why_ the cast to integer would be okay (so that people don't do it if it's not okay), but it seems sus, honestly.
author: workingjubilee

body:
I don't think this message is appropriate: if passing a mutable pointer is intentional, we should only suggest something which suppresses the warning, not something that changes the semantics of the `asm!`.

The problem here is that I don't see an obvious way to suppress the warning. Perhaps this lint would be better in clippy instead rather than something that generally applies to all Rust code?
author: Amanieu

author: Amanieu

body:
https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/pull/127063#discussion_r1674508742
> The problem here is that I don't see an obvious way to suppress the warning. Perhaps this lint would be better in clippy instead rather than something that generally applies to all Rust code?

At first, I wanted to make it an error, but probably some code would break and `asm!` is stable (could we jump on the edition2024 bandwagon?). Yeah, this is unsafe, and we can do a lot of stuff inside the `asm!` block, including freestyle transmute, however transmute does one job and *it* is dangerous, we can't do much with it besides "being smart" and looking for surrounding context, which is what clippy does with `eager_transmute` for example.

Here we could impose impose a simple rule that would help avoiding bugs with unintentional `nomem`. I can agree that the case with `*mut T` and `readonly` could be allowed, because we could pretend that the pointer is implicitly cast to `*const T` (like when calling functions that take `*const T`) and also the difference between `*mut` and `*const` is mostly cosmetic, but I don't see the same applying to `nomem` + `*const/mut T`.

Why would someone pass a pointer and do nothing with the data? If they need just the address, maybe they also need to consider if the provenance should be exposed or not. Idk, I think you know better than me how `asm!` is used, so if the final decision will be to not implement it here, then I won't insist. :thinking:

Yeah basically. As far as I'm aware we don't have any tests that ensure `FOO` actually ends up in the final binary. It won't, at least on msvc, because we define it as a COMDAT (i.e. we tell the linker it's allowed to remove it).

This is technically in keeping with the [documented behaviour](https://doc.rust-lang.org/stable/reference/abi.html?highlight=used#the-used-attribute) which only says the compiler considers it used, and not the linker. body:
> Is CaptureAll the new equivalent for OnlyOnFailure?

`CaptureAll` is essentially `OnlyOnFailure`, yes. I made the decision whether to print something during a command failure fully derived from other options, rather than configurable by users, because it was introducing unnecessary complexity to the command and it was only used in two places of bootstrap anyway. We should IMO always print failures, unless the failure is explicitly ignored.

> Also, I think we changed the variant names of this enum like 3 times already.. 😄

Well, refactoring is a continuous process, at least for me :) First I was trying to make the names as similar to the previous names used ad hoc in bootstrap code, to make it easier fo review that the migration is doing the same thing as before. Now that the usages of `BootstrapCmd` have been migrated, it was time to make the names better.

body:
Problem: so unfortunately, checking that the provided paths to `./x test` ends with an `rs` extension is both (1) an **overapproximation** and (2) an **underapproximation**.

1. **Overapproximation**: for example, the `rustdoc-js-std` test suite has primarily `js`-based tests and you can specify e.g. `./x test tests/rustdoc-js-std/parser-hof.js` and it would run that particular test.
2. **Underapproximation**: note that a file being `.rs` does not guarantee it is a test file; it can be an *auxiliary* file (support file), so the check presently would also miss passing an auxiliary `.rs` file.

I understand that this is a warning and is based on heuristics, but I wonder if we could try to be better here (so we don't generate misleading warnings, which I think is worse than not emitting a warning at all in this case).

I think something like the following logic may work (I need to do some experimenting myself):

1. Check if the provided path to a file has the test-suite-specific expected extension (e.g. `rs` for `ui`, `js` for `rustdoc-js-std`), otherwise easy bail.
2. If (1) succeeds, then we (somehow) panic in `run_tests` if 0 tests are run despite the pattern (of a path to a file) successfully matching.

Perhaps we can panic later when we perform test collection based on the pattern?

Let me know if you have any ideas.

body:
My thinking here is:
- We do need `NestedVisit::INTER = true`, so that `visit_item` is called.
  - The alternative would be to override `visit_nested_item` instead, which seems pointless because we would just be recreating the existing implementation anyway.
- Bodies of nested items don't actually get visited, because of the `visit_item` override.
- For any nested bodies that are not part of an item, we do want to visit any items contained within them.

body:
> And with generic "arguments" vs "parameters", the confusion is already in the names of the structs in the library, there is GenericArg, but also GenericParamDef, if we stick to 1 word, which should it be?

No, these are entirely different things. *Parameter* and *argument* (or equivalently *formal* and *actual* parameter) are well-established technical terms that have *precise* meanings.

> In the case of "calling convention" & "ABI", my idea was to use different synonyms for a concept to make them easier to understand if a person happens to better understand what's a calling convention than what's an ABI. I did the same thing with "bounds" & "constraints", I used to struggle with understanding Rust until I realised that a "bound" is simply a "constraint"

I appreciate the effort but I think we need to be a lot more careful here. Picking words and "synonyms" willy-nilly in the context of something as technical as a programming language hurts the quality of the docs in both the short and the long run. Indeed, "bound", "constraint", "restriction", "predicate", "clause" (to continue your example) may all refer to the same thing (natural languages are highly context-dependent, flexible and malleable after all) but as soon as we enter the world of jargon and technical language the rules change a bit and words that may have a relatively lax and general meaning may have a super specific meaning assigned to it inside a specific jargon. For example, take a look at "expression", "statement", "judgement", "type", "kind", "term", "value". Some of these words may be synonymous in everyday language but in the world of Rust, Haskell, programming language design or type theory these may refer to very concrete very precise ideas and concepts.

**I think the proper way to go about this would be to use the *precise* term as used by rustc and/or the Rust Reference and to optionally add a short explainer paragraph** (containing hyperlinks to more elaborate resources or one that draws comparisons to similar concepts etc.).

To get back to "bounds" and "constraints". In rustc, these terms are distinct. *Bounds* include *trait bounds* (`T: Trait`, `u32: for<'a> Trait<'a, Output = &'a ()>`) and outlives-bounds aka lifetime bounds (`T: 'a`, `'a: 'b`). Yes, in Haskell you would call that a "constraint" but in the Rust world you generally wouldn't (unless you're chatting with your peers where you likely won't speak in precise technical language) and `rustdoc_json_types` ought to be precise. `Output = &'a ()` would be a constraint OTOH, more specifically an associated item (equality) constraint where a constraint is either an equality or a *bound*. Furthermore, *clause* (`ty::Clause`) and *predicate* (`ty::Predicate`) are related but ultimately distinct concepts.
author: fmease

body:
And to clarify, my comment shouldn't be construed as taking a *prescriptive* stance, I'm very much a descriptivist. I'm very glad you've picked up the daunting task of documenting the entirety of this crate, that's very commendable!

Making use of well-established but still highly domain-specific terminology is not a form of *gate-keeping* as long as we define/document what we mean. It helps us establish a common language to talk about things in our environment. For one, it enables users of rustdoc-json-types to join the conversation of rustdoc and rustc devs, e.g., in issues, PRs, on Zulip etc.

body:
A few relevant things from https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man2/poll.2.html:

```text
The field events is an input parameter ...
This field may be specified as zero, in which case the only
events that can be returned in revents are POLLHUP, POLLERR, and
POLLNVAL (see below).
```

We probably don't need to set `POLLOUT` anymore as we aren't checking on it since https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/pull/45269.

```text
       POLLERR
              Error condition (only returned in revents; ignored in
              events).  This bit is also set for a file descriptor
              referring to the write end of a pipe when the read end has
              been closed.

       POLLHUP
              Hang up (only returned in revents; ignored in events).
              Note that when reading from a channel such as a pipe or a
              stream socket, this event merely indicates that the peer
              closed its end of the channel.  Subsequent reads from the
              channel will return 0 (end of file) only after all
              outstanding data in the channel has been consumed.

       POLLNVAL
              Invalid request: fd not open (only returned in revents;
              ignored in events).
```

From https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/issues/45265#issuecomment-336536875, it sounds like in reality it sets all three. 

The manpage doesn't say anything about setting an error to `SO_ERROR`. I would assume this is always true, but it does seem safer to have the fallback in place. It also seems a bit weird to me that we are checking only against POLLHUP and not a `POLLHUP | POLLNVAL | POLLERR` mask, since these are all documented error conditions (as you pointed out below. Possibly relevant only for files, but without checking kernel source seems uncertain).

Perhaps I just don't have all the context here, if you find docs on the `poll` / `SO_ERROR` relationship then please do link it.

---

So: I wouldn't really want to change the existing Linux handling to only check `take_error` because it means going from documented behavior to empirical behavior, even if has proven correct. In which case I would prefer the `cfg` suggestion above to the current proposal.

_However_ I think this code could be cleaned up a bit with the following, which should work on your system too:

1. Change the `libc::pollfd` struct constructed above to have events as 0 rather than `POLLOUT`, since we are no longer checking `POLLOUT` (since https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/pull/45269)
2. Because we are no longer have a possible `POLLOUT` `revent`, the possible results of `libc::poll` are:
    - -1: error via errno
    - 0: success
    - 3 (Linux), something else (vxworks): emitted revents, `POLLHUP | POLLNVAL | POLLERR`
3. Since we can no longer have any successful revents (previously `POLLOUT`), the last match arm can be changed to unconditionally emit an error (without checking `revents` or `Some(e) = take_error`). So just remove the `if` from the existing code so it always emits `self.take_error()?.unwrap_or_else(|| { ... })`.

   That is: that branch of the `match` will now always try to read the `SO_ERROR`, which works on both Linux and vxworks. If that fails, meaning revents were set but there is no `SO_ERROR` for some unexpected reason, it will emit an `Uncategorized` error (can never happen on vxworks per https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/issues/127018, but maybe possible on linux?).
4. If you feel like it, `debug_assert!` that the revents are something we expect so we learn if this isn't accurate.

If that tests well, then I think it might be a more robust option on all systems. If you make the changes please comment it well, somebody else is going to have to reverse engineer this one day...

---

Doesn't matter if the above works, but does Vxworks set `POLLNVAL` or `POLLERR` rather than a mask including `POLLHUP`?

body:
I disagree with this renaming, "attribute items" and "meta items" are different things and shouldn't be mixed.

Meta items (`struct MetaItem`) are a restricted subset of attribute items, used for working with built-in attributes in the compiler (most of which fit into that subset) as an implementation detail.

The `meta` matcher in macros matches attr items, not meta items, but we cannot just rename it because it's user-facing and stable.

`NtMeta` could be renamed to `NtAttrItem` to better match its essence rather than surface syntax, but why bother, it's removed in https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/pull/124141 anyway.
author: petrochenkov

author: petrochenkov

body:
The basic point is that the current naming of types with the compiler is bad. Off the top of your head, do you know the distinction between `NormalAttr::tokens` and `AttrItem::tokens`? I sure don't, I have to look at the comments every time.

Looking at the [reference](https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/attributes.html):

> InnerAttribute :
>    \# ! [ Attr ]
> 
> OuterAttribute :
>    \# [ Attr ]
> 
> Attr :
>    [SimplePath](https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/paths.html#simple-paths) AttrInput?
> 
> AttrInput :
>       [DelimTokenTree](https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/macros.html)
>    | = [Expression](https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/expressions.html)

So:
- "Attribute" is the whole thing, including the leading `#` and (if present) `!`. That's fine.
- "Attr" is the part within the brackets. That's a bad name, much too similar to "Attribute", and when "Attribute" is inevitably abbreviated to "Attr" they'll be indistinguishable. (I called this "Meta" in this PR which matches the `meta` fragment specifier, but is awkwardly close to the similar-but-slightly different "meta item".)
- "Attribute item" doesn't appear at all, either in this syntax or anywhere else on the page.
- "Meta item" is the restricted syntax used within the brackets for most builtin attributes. It's not a great name, but it's sufficiently different that it'll do.

The main problem is the lack of a good name for what the reference calls "Attr", i.e. the part within the brackets, not necessarily restricted to meta item syntax. That's the problem I'm trying to solve here. Something like "AttrContents" might work, and `NormalAttr::item` could become `NormalAttr::contents`. I want to avoid "item" as much as possible, it's too easily confused with normal [items](https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/items.html).
author: nnethercote

body:
> Something like "AttrContents" might work

The [meta section](https://veykril.github.io/tlborm/decl-macros/minutiae/fragment-specifiers.html#meta) of TLBORM says "The `meta` fragment matches the contents of an attribute".

body:
I think there are two serious contenders here.
- "Attribute"/"Meta"/"Meta item": what this PR does. Pros: "Meta" matches the `meta` fragment specifier. Cons: "Meta" and "MetaItem" are subtly different, which is potentially confusing.
- "Attribute"/"AttrContents"/"Meta item". Pros: clearer terminology. Cons: doesn't match `meta` fragment specifier.

body:
A niladic function would be one that takes zero arguments, a monadic function, one, a dyadic function, two, etc., by extension we arrive at variadic functions for a variable number of arguments. A function using C's `...` is indeed a variadic function. However, your example function will be called with 1 fixed argument and an unknown number of variable arguments. It is still a variadic function if no variable arguments are passed at all. It can, in those fixed parameters, accept arguments of types prohibited in the variable arguments. Differing from C's terminology seems fine, but the previous message was incorrect in any case.

I realize this is extremely pedantic, but we really ought to be at least a few notches more pedantic about how we handle varargs.

The preference in C/C++ compilers handling erroneous cases seems to be literally just calling it `...` which also seems fine, since that's what the programmer will actually be looking at. https://godbolt.org/z/81nEEEnjo

```
In file included from <source>:3:
<source>: In function 'void foo(int, ...)':
<source>:8:26: error: 'float' is promoted to 'double' when passed through '...' [-Werror]
    8 |     float f = va_arg(ap, float);
      |                          ^
<source>:8:26: note: (so you should pass 'double' not 'float' to 'va_arg')
<source>:8:26: note: if this code is reached, the program will abort
cc1plus: all warnings being treated as errors
Compiler returned: 1
```
author: workingjubilee

body:
**Edit: Responding to errs.**

To be fair, ``"can't pass `$ProblematicType` to variadic function"`` is imprecise (*incorrect* even, technically speaking) since it's legal to pass a value of $ProblematicType as an argument where the correp. param is "non-variable". E.g. `0f32` in `f(0f32, x, y, z)` is fine given e.g.`fn f(_: f32, ...)`.

Still, the new phrasing does feel a bit uncommon.
author: fmease

body:
...and this is an important distinction to preserve because some C ABIs are written in such a way that the way the arguments will be inspected in the callee function will be handled uniformly regardless of the number of arguments. In other words, they make it so `...` is ABI-compatible with a hypothetical function with the same fixed arguments. So they deliberately conflate "variadic function" with "a function receiving any number of arguments" i.e. including a function with 1 fixed argument or 10 fixed arguments, because the ABIs are identical.

**But others are not**, and the way varargs are passed has nothing to do with the way other args are passed, so this is in fact completely incompatible. On those platforms, code which conflates these will explode, and some C libraries had to be rewritten for those platforms.

body:
This arbitrary lookahead is also unnecessary. For structs, you need to look for a colon, for enums, you need to look for an identifier not followed by a colon. (either unit enum `enum X { A, B, C }` or with data `enum Y { D(E), F(G) }`, `enum Z { H { i: J } }`)

All of these happen under two tokens after the opening brace.

If you find a close brace before finding any of these characteristics, then a `struct` and a `enum` are both possible, so probably suggest both
author: fee1-dead

body:
I'd suggest look inside the parameters. If there are no parameters, e.g. `foo() {` / `foo();` you are expected to find a semicolon with only two bumps.

If there are, look for colons. If one writes `foo(x: u32)` we're pretty sure they are writing a function. If we find no colon before the closing parenthesis or before a comma `foo(x, y)` or `foo(x)`, then that looks like a function call. This can be done with up to two bumps since the opening parenthesis as well.

body:
It doesn't have any practical consequence. The new code has exactly the same variance and autotraits (at least built-in autotraits) as the old one. But different people prefer to use `PhantomData<T>` differently:

1. Some people set `T` to the _shortest_ possibility out of the set of all types that have the required variance and autotraits properties, or reach for a small set of ready-made idioms (usually short, which is why I am lumping this together). For example it's common to see `PhantomData<fn(U)>` (contravariant) or `PhantomData<fn(U) -> U>` (invariant) in data structures which have absolutely nothing to do with function pointers. These people decide what properties they want, then pick a type which hopefully delivers those properties.

2. Other people do the reverse: pick a type which mirrors what their data structure does the most closely, and hope that the correct variance and autotraits emerge from that for their data structure as a consequence. For example you might see `PhantomData<MutexGuard<'a, T>>` in a binding for some foreign language's mutex guard type, and the author can't even necessarily name what the resulting variances are.

3. A rare subgroup of both of the above is people who actually test the variance they're getting.

    ```rust
    fn f<'short, 'long: 'short>(x: MyType<'short>) -> MyType<'long> {
        x
    }

    fn g<'short, 'long: 'short>(x: MyType<'long>) -> MyType<'short> {
        x //~ lifetime may not live long enough
    }
    ```

4. The largest group: don't know / don't consider anything about variance and write whatever makes compilation succeed, even if it has incorrect variance.

`PhantomData<&'a u8>` is indicative of category 1 (_or_ 4, though I hope this would be unusual in standard library code) while `PhantomData<&'a [c_char]>` resembles category 2. I don't have an opinion about whether either is a better approach. 1 and 2 just have different failure modes.

This would make a bigger difference if support for nonstandard auto traits (https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/issues/13231) is ever stabilized. At that point all PhantomData usage would need to be audited, along the lines of https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/issues/13231#issuecomment-1399386472.

body:
Hm, remind me, are structs ever passed in registers in the Xtensa ABI? Some ABIs do, others do not.

Which registers is this notionally saving in the case of, say, the no-initial-args case (for `extern "C" fn(...)`, valid in all C implementations that adopt C23 and previously available as an extension in some)?

The reason I'm asking is because I want to know if this is one of those varargs ABIs where `extern "C" fn (c_int, ...)` where only 1 arg, a `c_int`, is passed, is ABI-equivalent to `extern "C" fn (c_int, c_int)` on entry into the actual function. Some ABIs deliberately design their varargs implementation to work like that, allowing you to basically deal with those two function pointers interchangeably. Others do not allow such because all varargs are handled in a distinct way so you only would match ABI details between varargs and other functions with only fixed args by accident.

( Obviously this also requires the varargs function itself to correctly "unpack" its arguments from the `va_list`. )
author: workingjubilee
workingjubilee

body:
Yes, structs can be passed via registers, structs can even be split across registers and stack space, _but_ primitive types will never be split. For instance, a `u128` either has to be all in registers, or all in stack never split across both.

> The reason I'm asking is because I want to know if this is one of those varargs ABIs where extern "C" fn (c_int, ...) where only 1 arg, a c_int, is passed, is ABI-equivalent to extern "C" fn (c_int, c_int) on entry into the actual function. Some ABIs deliberately design their varargs implementation to work like that, allowing you to basically deal with those two function pointers interchangeably. Others do not allow such because all varargs are handled in a distinct way so you only would match ABI details between varargs and other functions with only fixed args by accident.

From the Xtensa ISA:

![image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/f87fd0ec-0156-4e20-bd78-a97055c2e5e7)

So I believe in this case calling a normal function or vararg function is the same, but like you mentioned the function then has to unpack it's arguments in the vararg case.
